title: Mean Value Theorem & EVT
examples: When can I use the Mean Value Theorem?
How do I write the justification for the theorem?
What if the function is not continuous?

explain.say: Today we look at the Mean Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem. These theorems help us understand function behavior. We must check certain conditions before we can use them.

For the Mean Value Theorem, the function must be continuous on the closed interval. This means no breaks or holes are allowed between the endpoints. For example, the function f x squared plus one is continuous everywhere.

It must also be differentiable on the open interval. This means the function has no sharp corners or vertical tangents within the interval. Consider the function f x cubed which is differentiable everywhere.

The Extreme Value Theorem requires the function to be continuous on a closed interval. This guarantees that the function must have both a maximum and a minimum value. For instance, the function f x squared on zero to one is continuous.

When justifying a theorem, you must state the conditions are met. You must say the function is continuous and differentiable on the required intervals. For example, state that f x is continuous and differentiable on the interval.

faq.q: What does 'continuous on the closed interval' actually mean?
faq.a: It means you can draw the graph of the function from the start point to the end point without lifting your pencil. This is a fundamental requirement for both theorems.
asks: Is it okay if there is a jump in the graph?
What if the graph has a hole in it?

faq.q: If a function is differentiable, is it automatically continuous?
faq.a: Yes, if a function is differentiable at a point, it must also be continuous at that point. Differentiability is a stronger condition than just continuity.
asks: Can a function be differentiable but not continuous?

faq.q: What if the function is only defined on a small part of the interval?
faq.a: Both theorems require the function to be defined across the entire closed interval you are considering. You must check the domain first.
asks: Do both theorems need the function defined everywhere?
What if the domain is not closed?

faq.q: How do I write the justification wording correctly?
faq.a: You must explicitly state that the function meets all the necessary conditions listed for the theorem you are using. Just stating the math is not enough.
asks: What phrases should I use when justifying?
Do I need to prove the conditions are met?

faq.q: Does the Mean Value Theorem only apply to straight lines?
faq.a: No, it applies to any smooth curve over an interval. It guarantees a point where the tangent slope matches the average slope.
asks: Is this only for linear functions?
What does the theorem say about curves?

facts: The Mean Value Theorem relates the average rate of change to the instantaneous rate of change.
For MVT, the function must be continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open interval.
The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that a continuous function on a closed interval attains an absolute maximum and minimum.
The average rate of change is calculated using the slope formula: (f b minus f a) divided by (b minus a).

quiz.say: If f x equals x squared plus x on the interval zero to two, is the Mean Value Theorem applicable?

options.show: Only if the average rate is zero
options.say: Only if the average rate is zero

options.show: Only if the interval is zero to one
options.say: Only if the interval is zero to one

quiz.why: The function is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable everywhere, meeting the theorem's conditions.

wrong.0: This is tempting because you might forget to check the conditions, but the function is clearly smooth.
wrong.1: This confuses the theorem with finding roots, but the theorem applies regardless of the average rate.
wrong.2: The theorem works for any valid closed interval, not just zero to one.

quiz.say: For the Extreme Value Theorem to apply to f x equals sin x on the interval negative pi to pi, what must be true?

options.show: The interval must have zero length.
options.say: The interval must have zero length.

options.show: The function must be continuous on the closed interval.
options.say: The function must be continuous on the closed interval.

quiz.why: Sine is a smooth, continuous wave, so the theorem guarantees both a maximum and a minimum value on this range.

wrong.0: This confuses the requirement with a single point, but the interval length can be anything positive.
wrong.1: The theorem applies to many non-linear functions, not just straight lines.
wrong.2: While differentiability implies continuity, the EVT only strictly requires continuity.

quiz.say: A function is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b). What must you do when justifying the use of the Mean Value Theorem?

options.show: Only calculate the average rate of change.
options.say: Only calculate the average rate of change.

options.show: Check if the function is always increasing.
options.say: Check if the function is always increasing.

options.show: Show that the derivative equals zero somewhere.
options.say: Show that the derivative equals zero somewhere.

options.show: State that the function is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b).
options.say: State that the function is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b).

quiz.why: Proper justification means explicitly confirming that both the continuity and differentiability conditions are met for the given interval.

wrong.0: Calculating the rate is the goal, but you must first prove you are allowed to calculate it.
wrong.1: The function can decrease and still satisfy the Mean Value Theorem.
wrong.2: Setting the derivative to zero finds critical points, which is different from applying MVT.
